title: Nghỉ chăm con cho cha · Agree / Disagree
prompt: Some people believe that reserving part of paid parental leave exclusively for fathers should be a priority. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
instructions: Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

grammar.why: Trong câu “In conclusion, protected time for fathers is a worthwhile priority when it changes everyday caregiving; adequate income replacement makes that opportunity real rather than merely statutory.”, while nối hai diễn biến hoặc yêu cầu cần xét cùng nhau; ở đây phải giữ cả hai phía để không biến điều kiện giới hạn thành phủ nhận toàn bộ lợi ích. paragraphs: Reserved parental leave concerns who actually performs care, rather than simply how many weeks a family receives. I support reserving paid leave for fathers, provided replacement pay and employment protection enable families across income groups to use it.

Dedicated leave can make caring responsibilities less unequal. An entitlement that cannot simply transfer to mothers gives fathers time to develop everyday caregiving skills. A father could take several weeks of routine care after the other parent returns to work. Practice in routine care can change what each parent knows and is expected to do, rather than leave fathers in an occasional supporting role.

Low replacement pay can make leave unusable for families dependent on the higher earner's income. An entitlement paid well below normal earnings can be unusable where the father supplies most household income. Families may preserve the mother's larger share of care simply because they cannot absorb the loss, leaving the reserved weeks formally available but largely untaken. Pay levels and employment protection should make the entitlement financially realistic. Adequate pay and job protection must accompany non-transferability, because a formally individual entitlement has little effect when household finances make using it unrealistic. Employers should publish return-to-work arrangements before leave begins, allowing fathers to take responsibility for care without having to negotiate continued employment from a vulnerable position after their absence. Developing a second competent carer can benefit the family long after leave ends, but an entitlement that households cannot afford to use produces no comparable change.
In conclusion, protected time for fathers is a worthwhile priority when it changes everyday caregiving; adequate income replacement makes that opportunity real rather than merely statutory.
